intro: Cyprus is not a walk. These four trees sit in two districts an hour or more apart by car, and none of them is within reach of another on foot. Three stand beside a chapel, a monastery or a country church, which is not a coincidence: sacred ground is where old trees survive, and it also means nobody charges to see them. The biggest claim belongs to an olive at Xyliatos, thirteen metres round and wider than it is tall.
meta_description: Cyprus's four remarkable trees: an olive at Xyliatos thirteen metres round, and a plane the national post office put on a stamp.
question_meta: Cyprus's oldest tree is the olive at Xyliatos, given as 800 to 1,700 years. Why nobody can settle the figure, and what else is worth the drive.
question_answer: The oldest tree on this Cyprus list is the old olive at Potima in Xyliatos, in the Nicosia district foothills, and its age is unsettled: sources give it as anywhere from 800 to 1,700 years. The Xyliatos Community Council, which had it placed under Department of Forests protection in 2004, says about 1,700 years; a Cypriot tourism site says 800. Neither figure comes from a ring count, and the same is true of every age on this page. What is measured is the trunk: thirteen metres round, the largest recorded girth of any olive on the island.
question_context: Nobody has counted a ring on any of these four trees. Every age here is a received figure passed between village councils, tourism pages and a postage stamp, and where two sources disagree the gap is wide: 800 years against 1,700 for the Xyliatos olive, a thousand years against a few centuries for the laurel at Pente Litharia, 800 against 1,200 for the plane at Ayia Mavri. Olives are the hardest of all to date, because the old heartwood rots out and the trunk splits into separate living strips, leaving nothing continuous to count. What can be measured is girth, and the Xyliatos olive's thirteen metres is the largest recorded on the island, which is the practical reason it holds the title. The Cyprus Department of Forests placed both that olive and the Ayia Mavri plane under protection in 2004. The oak at Kalopanagiotis and the laurel at Pente Litharia carry the better stories, one said to have hidden a chapel from raiders and the other said to be left over from a shrine to Apollo, but neither has an age anyone has tested. If you have a tape measure and a spare afternoon, tell us.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Cyprus?
faq.a: On this list, the old olive at Potima in Xyliatos, given as 800 years by one source and about 1,700 by the village council that had it protected. Its trunk is thirteen metres round, the largest recorded girth of any olive on Cyprus, which is the one figure nobody argues about.

faq.q: Do you need a car to see these trees?
faq.a: Yes. All four stand in Troodos foothill villages with no useful bus service, and they split across two districts: the oak at Kalopanagiotis and the olive at Xyliatos in the Nicosia district, the laurel near Omodos and the plane near Koilani in the Limassol district. Each pair is a comfortable half day by car.

faq.q: Are Cyprus's ancient trees free to visit?
faq.a: All four here are. Three stand beside a chapel, a monastery or a country church, on open ground with no gate and no ticket, and the olive at Xyliatos grows in the open within the village. Daylight hours, and nobody to ask.

faq.q: What about the cedars of Cedar Valley?
faq.a: Cedar Valley in the Paphos Forest holds one of the world's largest stands of Cedrus brevifolia, the Cyprus cedar, with counts running from 16,000 mature trees at Tripylos to 130,000 across the wider valley. It is a forest walk rather than a tree to stand in front of: no individual cedar there is named, signposted or separately designated, which is why none appears on this list.

trees.name: The Sacred Oak of Theoskepasti

location.address: Chapel of Panagia Theoskepasti, beside the Agios Ioannis Lampadistis Monastery, Kalopanagiotis, Marathasa valley, Nicosia district, Cyprus

trees.story: The chapel next door is named after what this tree is said to have done. Panagia Theoskepasti means God-covered, and the account told in Kalopanagiotis is that the oak's branches spread far enough over the small 12th century chapel to hide it from raiders passing through the Marathasa valley. Tradition rather than record, but it has carried the name for a long time. The tree is a prinos, the Cypriot word for kermes oak, though one account of the site calls it a holm oak instead, a related but different species, and nobody has settled which it is. If you can tell the two apart on sight, tell us. Local tradition puts the oak at roughly 700 years. Every source repeats that figure and none of them measured it, so read it as a claim rather than a count. What is on record is that the Cyprus Department of Forests holds the tree under protection. It stands in the open yard beside the chapel, a few steps from the Agios Ioannis Lampadistis Monastery, which UNESCO listed in 1985 among the Painted Churches of the Troodos Region. Kalopanagiotis sits on the northern flank of Troodos, about an hour of mountain road from Nicosia, and the oak asks nothing of a visitor: no gate, no ticket, daylight hours.
trees.access: Free. Stands in the open yard beside a public chapel next to the UNESCO-listed monastery complex; no permission needed, open in daylight.
trees.transport: No public transport reaches Kalopanagiotis usefully; by car roughly 50 km / 60-70 minutes from Nicosia via the Troodos foothill roads.
trees.notes: Two independent tourism/heritage sources (cyprusisland.net, cypriot-villages.uk) agree: a huge 'prinos' oak grew beside the 12th-century Theoskepasti chapel (built alongside Agios Ioannis Lampadistis Monastery, itself part of the 1985 UNESCO Painted Churches of the Troodos Region listing) and its branches grew to shield the chapel from raiders' sight, which is where the name Theoskepasti ('God-covered') comes from. Both sources say the tree is under protection of the Cyprus Department of Forests. Species naming is inconsistent across sources: 'prinos' (Greek for Kermes oak, Quercus coccifera) is the term both sources use, but one nearby account also calls it 'holm oak', a related but distinct species (Quercus ilex); shipped as Kermes Oak (Quercus coccifera) with the ambiguity flagged and stated in the story. The verify pass delivered the species string as 'Kermes Oak, locally "prinos" (Quercus coccifera, possibly Quercus ilex)'; normalised to the canonical single-name form for species grouping (hard rule 9), the ambiguity carried in prose instead. Age of '700 years' is a repeated local legend/tourism figure, not a Forest Department measurement or growth-rate derivation; no girth figure found. Location is chapel/monastery-yard level, not a tree-level coordinate; the coordinate given is the centre of the road named after the monastery (OSM), roughly 100-150m precision. Wikipedia's 'Church of Panagia Theoskepasti' article is a DIFFERENT, unrelated church in Kato Paphos and does not corroborate this tree; do not cite it as a source for this entry. A third source, a Russian-language Cyprus blog (dom.com.cy), independently repeats the same 700-year figure and legend, but was not counted as one of the two independent sources since its editorial content appears derivative of tourism copy.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the branches spreading over the small chapel of Panagia Theoskepasti, which is named for exactly that. It stands in the open yard beside the Agios Ioannis Lampadistis monastery.

trees.name: The Old Olive Tree of Xyliatos

location.address: Potima, Xyliatos village, Nicosia district, Cyprus

trees.story: This olive is wider around than it is tall. Thirteen metres of trunk circumference against a height of about six, which is roughly what an olive does when it is given enough centuries: the trunk splits, hollows and fuses back on itself while the crown stays low and hard. It is held to be the largest-girth olive on Cyprus, and the oldest. How old is exactly the argument. The Xyliatos Community Council, which campaigned to have the tree protected, says about 1,700 years. A Cypriot tourism site says 800. Neither shows any working, no ring count and no growth-rate calculation, and olives are close to impossible to date anyway, because the old heartwood rots out and leaves nothing continuous to read. Both figures are received, so the honest answer is the range. What is documented is 2004, the year the Department of Forests placed the tree under protection after the council pressed for it. On the council's figure the olive was already old under Byzantine rule and would have stood through Richard the Lionheart's sale of the island in 1191, the Lusignan and Venetian centuries and three hundred years of Ottoman administration. On the tourism figure it starts around that same 1191. It grows in the open at Potima, a named spot in the village, in the foothills near the Xyliatos dam.
trees.access: Free, standing in the open in the Potima area of the village; no permission needed.
trees.transport: No useful public transport; by car roughly 25 km / 35-40 minutes from Nicosia, in the Troodos foothills near the Xyliatos dam and forest.
trees.notes: Two independent sources agree this is regarded as the oldest and largest-girth olive tree in Cyprus, standing at 'Potima' in Xyliatos village, and that it was placed under Department of Forests protection in 2004 after the Xyliatos Community Council's own efforts. Both agree on circumference/girth of 13 metres (girth_cm 1300). AGE DISAGREES SHARPLY: the Xyliatos Community Council's own site (the more authoritative, official source) states approximately 1,700 years; cyprusisland.net, a tourism site, states 800 years. Neither cites a growth-ring count or other derivation, both read as received local figures, so the entry is flagged and the page states the range rather than picking one. HEIGHT DISCREPANCY, resolved: cyprusisland.net says 'height of 60 metres', which is physically impossible for an olive tree and is very likely a copy error; the official Xyliatos Community Council site gives height 6 metres for the same tree, which is plausible and is treated as correct. The 60m figure is not published anywhere on this page. Location: 'Potima' is a named place within the village; the coordinates used (35.03175, 33.03505) come from a Wikiloc GPS trail titled 'Giant olive tree 1700 yrs old Xyliatos Nicosia Cyprus', extracted via search snippet only, wikiloc.com itself returned HTTP 403 to both WebFetch and curl with a browser user agent (two attempts, both blocked) so the page was never directly viewed; treat the coordinate as a reasonable trail-waypoint estimate rather than a confirmed tree-level pin, hence approximate precision. wikimapia.org's 'Giant Olive Tree' page returned only a JS cookie-redirect stub to curl, no usable coordinates, one attempt, not retried.

best_time.label: September to November: the harvest, when the fruit turns from green to black

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by being wider than it is tall: thirteen metres of split and fused trunk under a crown only about six metres up. It stands in the open in the Potima area of Xyliatos.

trees.name: The Ancient Laurel of Apostle Philip
trees.age_estimate: roughly 1,000 years by one source, only 'a few centuries' by another

location.address: Beside the country Chapel of Apostle Philip, Pente Litharia (Five Rocks), about 3 km west of Omodos village, Limassol district, Cyprus

trees.story: Bay laurel is the herb in the kitchen cupboard, usually a shrub and rarely a tree of any size. This one is eight metres around. It stands at Pente Litharia, Five Rocks, about three kilometres west of Omodos down a minor road, beside the oldest of that village's country churches, the Chapel of Apostle Philip. How old the laurel is depends on who is asked, and the two answers are far apart. A Limassol heritage site calls it roughly 1,000 years. Omodos's own village site will say only that it is a few centuries. Neither counts rings, so the vaguer figure stays vague here rather than being sharpened into the flattering one. Local tradition holds that the site was a shrine to Apollo before it was Christianised, and points at the laurel as what survived the change, laurel being the tree sacred to Apollo in Greek myth. Both accounts repeat that story and neither is archaeology. What is dated is the building: the chapel was renovated in 1773. Height is given as 17 metres on one page and 10 metres on another from the same source, so take the crown as tall rather than measured. It stands in open country with no gate, no ticket and nobody to ask, which is roughly how it has been since somebody first decided this spot was worth a chapel.
trees.access: Free, standing beside a small rural chapel in the open countryside; no permission needed. Reached by an unpaved/minor road about 3 km west of Omodos village; no gate or restriction mentioned by either source.
trees.transport: No public transport; by car about 3 km from Omodos village (itself roughly 55 km / 60-75 minutes from Limassol), on rural roads.
trees.notes: Two independent sources agree: a large, ancient bay laurel stands beside the country Chapel of Apostle Philip at 'Pente Litharia' (Five Rocks), the oldest of Omodos's rural chapels, about 3km west of the village. Both give identical measurements: circumference 8 metres, height 17 metres (girth_cm 800). Both note local tradition that the site was originally a shrine to Apollo before Christianisation, with the laurel (sacred to Apollo in Greek myth) cited as a surviving trace; this is a historical/legendary claim repeated by both sources, not an archaeological fact, and reads as tradition in the story. AGE DIFFERS: allaboutlimassol.com gives 'approximately 1000 years old'; omodos.org, the village's own site, is vaguer, 'estimated to be a few centuries'. Neither cites a derivation (no growth rate or ring count), so both are received figures; flagged, and the vaguer official figure is deliberately not sharpened. Chapel was renovated in 1773 per both sources, which is a fact about the building, not the tree (avoiding a bridge claim), and the story states it that way. A THIRD allaboutlimassol.com page (their Limassol trees survey) independently gives this same tree as 'the laurel tree in Omodos village, 1.000 years old... 10 meters tall', which CONTRADICTS the dedicated chapel page's height of 17 metres; both pages are on the same domain so this is an internal inconsistency rather than a second confirming source, flagged, height 17m kept as the dedicated-page figure and the discrepancy stated on the page. LOCATION: no source gives coordinates for the chapel itself; Nominatim and an Overpass search for a place of worship named 'Philip' near Omodos returned nothing. The coordinate recorded here is OMODOS VILLAGE CENTRE, not the tree, offset roughly 3km east of the true site; a future pass with satellite imagery or a visit should pin the actual chapel. Village-level precision only, marked approximate for that reason specifically.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as a bay laurel grown to eight metres round, where the species is usually a kitchen shrub. It stands beside the little Chapel of Apostle Philip at Pente Litharia, west of Omodos.

trees.name: The Plane Tree of Ayia Mavri
trees.age_estimate: roughly 800 years by two sources, 1,200 by a third

location.address: Beside the Ayia Mavri chapel, on the Kryos river, on the road between Koilani and Pera Pedi (about 2 km from Koilani), Limassol district, Cyprus
location.neighbourhood: Between Koilani and Pera Pedi, Krasochoria wine region

trees.story: Cyprus put this tree on a postage stamp. The national post office's Centennial Trees of Cyprus series records the Oriental plane at Ayia Mavri as about 800 years old, with a trunk 8.20 metres round and a crown reaching 38 metres, and notes that it was formally designated for protection in 2004. A Limassol heritage survey, working from its own measurements, gives the same age and close to the same figures, 8 metres and 36. A third Cypriot site says 1,200 years instead and offers no measurements at all, so the age sits between two sources that agree and one that does not. Planes want their feet wet, which explains the address: the bank of the Kryos river, beside the small Ayia Mavri chapel, on the road linking Koilani to Pera Pedi through the Krasochoria, the wine villages of the southern Troodos. Platanus orientalis is the eastern Mediterranean's own plane, the species that shades village squares from Greece to Anatolia and one parent of the London plane that later took over northern European cities. On the lower estimate this tree was already growing when the Lusignan kings ruled Cyprus, and it has stood through the Venetian, Ottoman and British administrations since. Free, open, and about forty minutes of hill road from Limassol.
verified_sources: https://www.cypruspost.post/en/centennial-trees (Cyprus Post centennial trees stamp issue: Agia Mavri Oriental Plane, girth at breast height 8.20 m, 38 m high, about 800 years, declared protected 2004)
trees.access: Free, standing in the open beside a small rural riverside chapel; no permission needed. Reached by the road connecting Koilani and Pera Pedi villages.
trees.transport: No public transport; by car about 30 km / 40-45 minutes from Limassol, in the Krasochoria wine-village region of the Troodos foothills.
trees.notes: Two independent sources: Cyprus Post's own 'Centennial Trees of Cyprus' stamp-series page (cypruspost.post, a national postal-service publication, effectively an official/semi-official listing) gives this Oriental Plane at Agia Mavri as approximately 800 years old, trunk circumference 8.20m, height 38m, and states it was DESIGNATED (protected) in 2004. allaboutlimassol.com's Limassol trees survey independently corroborates: 'the plane tree at Ayia Mavri in Kilani, aged 800 years old... trunk is 8 meters wide and it reached up to 36 meters high' (on the way from Pera Pedi to Kilani/Koilani village); the two sources agree closely on age, girth and height (minor rounding: 8m vs 8.20m; 36m vs 38m; 'wide' may mean diameter rather than circumference, a units ambiguity worth flagging, but the circumference figure from the more precise Cyprus Post source is used). A THIRD source, cyprusisland.net's own Ayia Mavri Chapel page, instead calls it '1200 years old' with no size given and no designation-year claim; this conflicts with the two agreeing sources, so the age is flagged and both figures are recorded and published rather than one chosen silently. Local legend (in the cyprusisland.net source only, not corroborated) ties the chapel's name to a saint named Mavri who parted rock to help a fleeing couple; this is folklore, not fact, and concerns the chapel rather than the tree, so it is not used to date the tree (avoiding a bridge claim) and is not in the story. LOCATION: no source gives exact coordinates; the chapel sits on the Kryos river roughly 2km from Koilani toward Pera Pedi. The coordinate recorded is Koilani village centre (OSM), not the tree itself; Overpass searches for a place of worship named 'Mavri' near the villages returned nothing. Marked approximate for that reason.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 8.20 metres round, under a crown reaching close to 38 metres. It stands on the bank of the Kryos river beside the small Ayia Mavri chapel.

trees.name: The Ayia Napa Monastery sycamore fig

location.address: Outside the south gate of Ayia Napa Monastery, Archbishop Makarios III Square, Ayia Napa 5330

location_site.name: Ayia Napa Monastery south gate forecourt

trees.story: In the middle of Ayia Napa, a town better known for its beaches and clubs, stands a fig tree said to be more than 600 years old. It is a sycamore fig, Ficus sycomorus, the fig of Egypt and the Bible, which Cypriots call toumbezia, and it grows in the forecourt outside the south gate of Ayia Napa Monastery. The Department of Forests lists a sycamore fig in Ayia Napa as a natural monument, 7.05 metres round and 26 metres tall, with an estimated age that comes to a little over 600 today. That listing gives no address, and two younger figs in the town are on it as well, so matching it to this tree rests on the village and the age rather than on anything written down. Every visitor source puts this one at over 600. The story told at the monastery is that a Venetian noblewoman from Famagusta took refuge in the cave here, founded the monastery and planted the fig; one guide makes her an abbess instead. That is tradition, not record. One claim needs correcting. A Famagusta tourism page calls this the oldest tree in Cyprus, but the olive at Xyliatos and the terebinth at Apesia are both given greater ages, so it is not. The monastery behind it is a museum now. The fig is still the shade in front of it.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, which a visitor guide says takes three or four people to circle. It stands in the forecourt just outside the south gate of Ayia Napa Monastery, on the main square.

official_register.name: Μνημεία της φύσης, Τμήμα Δασών (Department of Forests, Cyprus)

trees.access: Free. The fig stands in the open forecourt outside the monastery's south gate, on the main square, and can be seen at any hour. The monastery behind it is a museum with free admission, about 09:30 to 15:00 in winter and 09:30 to 21:00 in summer; check before relying on those times.
trees.transport: In the centre of Ayia Napa beside the main square; the 'Agia Napa Monastery 1' and '2' bus stops on Archiepiskopou Makariou III are about 100 m away.

trees.name: The lone juniper of Cape Greco

location.address: Cape Greco National Forest Park, open field near the Sea Caves, Ayia Napa 5340

trees.pin_source: Commons photo geotag agreeing with komoot
trees.story: Nobody has dated this juniper and nobody has measured it, and wedding photographers come to it anyway. It stands alone in the middle of an open field in Cape Greco National Forest Park, the headland at the south-eastern tip of Cyprus, a few minutes on foot from the Sea Caves, and a Cypriot magazine piece from August 2026 names it a favourite spot for wedding pictures. One listing calls it the Tree of Cape Greco, another the Tree of Life. A travel site goes further and calls it one of the biggest and most photographed trees in Cyprus, which is the kind of thing travel sites say; there is no figure behind the first half of that. The species comes from a hiking app, where a user titled it Phoenician juniper, Juniperus phoenicea, and every other source simply says juniper. That is the low, tough conifer of Mediterranean coasts and cliffs, and listings here describe this one as windswept, which is easy to believe of a single tree in an open field on an exposed cape. Walkers have been writing it up as alive and well every year since at least 2022, and there is a bench beside it for anyone who wants to sit with the view. Its age is the open question. If you know when it was first noticed here, or what the trunk measures, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the solitary tree in the middle of an open field, with a bench beside it. It stands a few minutes' walk from the Sea Caves in Cape Greco National Forest Park.
trees.access: Free. It stands in an open field inside Cape Greco National Forest Park, a few minutes' walk from the Sea Caves, with a bench beside it.
trees.transport: By car about 10 minutes from Ayia Napa or Protaras to the park, then a short walk; a walker reports a bus stop nearby.

trees.name: The Anglisides Olive Museum olive

location.address: Olive Museum yard, Agiou Amvrosiou, Anglisides 7571, Larnaca District

trees.story: In 2004 the Cyprus Mail reported that this olive's hollow trunk had room for ten people inside. The trunk split early in its life and opened into a chamber of about three square metres, and at some point the split was widened with stacked bricks. Outside, the Department of Forests measures it at 10.35 metres round, under a crown only about six metres high. The register records the olive as proclaimed a natural monument on 30 January 2004, and a week later the Cyprus Mail was still describing the protection as a proposal. How old it is depends on the source. The register's estimate comes to a little over 700 years, and a village guide and the Olive Museum both say about 700. The 2004 article said almost 1,000. Olives rot from the inside, so there is no ring count to settle it, and the honest answer sits somewhere between the two. On the lower figure it was already growing while the Lusignan kings ruled Cyprus. The same article placed the tree on land belonging to a local family. Today the village's Olive Museum lists one of the island's oldest olives in its yard, and we take that to be this tree, matched by village and age rather than by any document joining the two. No dated recent photograph has turned up either. If you have seen it standing lately, tell us. For the record, the olive at Xyliatos is wider, at thirteen metres round.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the hollow, split trunk, 10.35 metres round under a crown only about six metres high. It stands in the yard of the Olive Museum in Anglisides.

official_register.name: Μνημεία της φύσης, Τμήμα Δασών (Department of Forests, Cyprus)

trees.access: In the Olive Museum yard, open Monday to Friday 08:00 to 14:00 and closed on public holidays. Any fee is not published. A 2004 report placed the tree on private family land, so ask at the museum that the yard tree is the old one before making the trip.
trees.transport: No public transport found; by car about 17 km south-west of Larnaca.

trees.name: The Oak of Laneia

location.address: North of Laneia village, Limassol District, Cyprus

trees.story: Laneia used to have two famous oaks. The one with the legend, the Royal Oak, under which a Henry of France is said to have rested, came down, by some accounts in 1997, and only a remnant of it survives. This is the one still standing. It grows in a quiet patch of wild vegetation just north of Laneia, a wine village in the hills above Limassol, and it is an Aleppo oak, Quercus infectoria subsp. veneris, the island's form of the gall oak of the eastern Mediterranean. The numbers depend on who held the tape. A Limassol guide gives 8.4 metres round and 26 metres tall, with a big hollow on the east side, and a naturalist who photographed it in March 2026 recorded the same 8.4 metres. An International Oak Society report from the same spring counts it among three famous large oaks of Cyprus. The Department of Forests register, which proclaimed it a natural monument in 2004, says 6.10 metres round and 7 tall instead. The gap is wide enough that the register may be describing a different measurement, or even a different trunk, so the girth here is the one two observers agree on. The age is broad too, about 600 years on the register's estimate and over 800 in the guide, with no ring count behind either. Nobody has published who owns the ground around it, so keep to paths and verges on the way in.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about 8.4 metres round, with a big hollow on its east side. It stands among wild vegetation just north of Laneia village.

official_register.name: Μνημεία της φύσης, Τμήμα Δασών (Department of Forests, Cyprus)

trees.access: No source says who owns the ground; the register lists it as unknown. A tourism guide describes a quiet spot north of the village among wild vegetation, and a naturalist reached and photographed the tree in March 2026. Keep to paths and verges and respect any fence.
trees.transport: By car about 24 km north-west of Limassol into the wine villages; no bus service found.

trees.name: The Terebinth of Apesia
trees.story: No tree on the Cyprus government's register of tree monuments is given a greater age than this one, about 1,500 years. The Department of Forests made it a natural monument in 2004, and when the national post office put it on a stamp in its Centennial Trees series it used the same figures, a trunk 6.80 metres round, a crown 10 metres high and about a millennium and a half. Hold that number loosely. It is an estimate, not a count, and one botanical source points out that no Atlas pistachio has been reliably dated beyond about 600 years, and that a big trunk tends to inflate the guess. So the honest range runs from several centuries to the register's fifteen centuries. The village is not troubled by any of this. The island's tourism site introduces Apesia, about 480 metres up in the hills north of Limassol, as the village of the old tremithos, the Cypriot name for the tree, and locals call it the Tremithos of Ai Yorkos, dedicated to Saint George. A Limassol guide says it is the first thing you see on entering the village and calls it one of the oldest of its species in the world. Another site puts it in the courtyard of the old elementary school, built in 1911. Those may well be the same spot. We have not pinned it, so the map marks the village. If you know exactly where it stands, tell us and the pin moves.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the big Atlas pistachio, 6.80 metres round and about 10 metres tall, that locals call the Tremithos of Ai Yorkos. It stands in Apesia, by one account in the old school courtyard.

official_register.name: Μνημεία της φύσης, Τμήμα Δασών (Department of Forests, Cyprus)

trees.access: Free to see. Sources place it in the village, either at the entrance or in the courtyard of the old elementary school; the exact spot is unconfirmed, so ask in the village.
trees.transport: No public transport found. By car from Limassol on the B8 toward Troodos, then the F812 near the Church of Saint Irene to Apesia.

trees.name: The Lagoudera Oak at Panagia tou Araka

location.address: Panagia tou Araka church yard, Lagoudera, Nicosia District (Pitsilia)

location_site.name: Panagia tou Araka church yard, Lagoudera

trees.story: The frescoes in the church beside this oak are dated 1192, and one local account says the tree went in when the church was built. Panagia tou Araka, on the slopes above Lagoudera in the Pitsilia hills, is one of the painted Byzantine churches of Troodos that UNESCO listed in 1985, and the Department of Forests' own trail leaflet has walkers meet the oak as they enter its yard at the end of the nature trail from Stavros tou Agiasmati. The leaflet names it an Aleppo oak, Quercus infectoria subsp. veneris, about 800 years old, a declared nature monument in the Department's care. The register, which proclaimed it in 2011, gives 700 years, 4.55 metres round and 16 metres tall, and the island's tourism site also says 700. None of those figures comes from a ring count, so read it as seven or eight centuries, both of them estimates. On either one it has stood beside those frescoes for most of their life, through Lusignan, Venetian, Ottoman and British rule. One travel site puts the tree about a hundred metres south of the church rather than at its entrance, so look by the gate first and a little further south if it is not there. Recent proof is thin. No dated photograph of the trunk from the last few years has turned up, only one from 1992 in a university collection. If you have been, a dated picture would settle it.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the big oak, 4.55 metres round and 16 metres tall, that walkers meet on entering the yard of Panagia tou Araka. One account places it about 100 metres south of the church instead.

official_register.name: Μνημεία της φύσης, Τμήμα Δασών (Department of Forests, Cyprus)

trees.access: Free to see from the yard of Panagia tou Araka, at the entrance by most accounts. Church opening hours are not confirmed (one listing says 09:00 to 18:00); inside the church, shoulders and knees covered.
trees.transport: No public transport found to Lagoudera. By car to the church, or on foot along the Department of Forests' nature trail from Stavros tou Agiasmati, which ends in the church yard.

trees.name: The Giant Black Pine of Troodos

location.address: On the Artemis nature trail, Troodos National Forest Park, below Mount Olympus (Chionistra), Limassol District

trees.story: By the Forestry Department's own sign, this pine was already a young tree when Magellan set out across the Pacific in the early sixteenth century. The sign stands at the trunk on the Artemis trail, the seven-kilometre loop around Chionistra, the summit of Mount Olympus and the highest ground in Cyprus, and it puts the tree at more than 500 years old. It is a black pine, Pinus nigra subsp. pallasiana, the eastern form of the species, and walkers know it as the Giant Black Pine. A hiking app marks it about 400 metres in from the start of the loop and describes a very imposing pine with a huge trunk next to the pines around it. It is not alone in its age. The same sign says a fair number of protected pines like it survive on the highest parts of the Troodos National Forest Park, and that the oldest is about 1,000 years, which matches the Department of Forests' leaflet giving the black pines up here 500 to 1,000 years. The trail's official listing mentions two of them on this loop, about 500 years old, without saying which. Nobody has published a girth or a height for this one. If you walk it with a tape, that would be the first number on record. The loop itself is easy and signposted, and it carries on round the mountain after the giant.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the huge trunk, far bigger than the pines around it, and the Forestry Department sign at its foot. It stands beside the Artemis trail about 400 metres from the start of the loop.
trees.access: Free. On the Artemis trail inside the Troodos National Forest Park, open to walkers: an easy, signposted circular trail of about 7 km whose start is about 300 m from the junction of the Chionistra road and the Troodos-Prodromos road. The pine stands near the start of the loop.
trees.transport: No public transport found. By car to the Artemis trail start near Troodos, about 300 m from the Chionistra and Prodromos road junction, then about 400 m on foot along the loop.

trees.name: The Pano Platres Oak

location.address: Dirt road off the B8 about 1.5 km east of Platres, Pano Platres, Limassol District

trees.story: Oak specialists know this tree as Cyprus 505, the same number as its girth in centimetres. The International Oak Society's report from a trip in spring 2026 records a trunk 5.05 metres round and 1.60 across, a canopy 30 metres wide and a height of more than 25, and calls it a perfectly vital oak with no sign of breakage or decline. It is an Aleppo oak, Quercus infectoria subsp. veneris, standing at the end of a lane in Pano Platres, the upper part of the hill resort on the southern slopes of Troodos. The Department of Forests made it a natural monument in 2004 and gives it about two centuries. Its register entry also gives a girth of 1.40 metres, which is very probably the diameter written in the girth column, and a trunk of five metres in this species leaves room for an older tree than the register allows. Nobody has worked that out properly, so the age here stays at the register's figure, over two centuries, with the upper end left open. Hotel pages nearby advertise a 700-year-old oak; nothing we have read supports that. The register lists only one oak for the village, and the lane matches a visitor listing's directions to a 200-year-old oak 1.5 km east of Platres, so this is very likely that tree, though no source joins the two in writing. The ground at the end of the lane may be private.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 5.05 metres round, under a crown about 30 metres across. It stands at the end of a dirt lane off the B8, about 1.5 km east of Platres, on the edge of a plot.

official_register.name: Μνημεία της φύσης, Τμήμα Δασών (Department of Forests, Cyprus)

trees.access: At the end of a dirt lane on the edge of a plot, reached from the B8 about 1.5 km east of Platres, with limited parking. No official source says the lane or the ground is open to visitors and it may be private; look from the lane if there is a sign or fence.
trees.transport: No public transport found; about 1.5 km by road from Platres village centre, walkable along the B8.

trees.name: The Agia Solomoni wishing tree

location.address: Agia Solomoni Catacomb, Kato Paphos, Paphos

trees.story: This tree is dressed in other people's handkerchiefs. Hundreds of strips of cloth, scarves and the odd face mask hang from its branches, with a few small padlocks among them, left as offerings to Saint Solomoni at the catacomb directly beneath it. Many visitors believe the tree helps with eye trouble; the national tourism site says only that it is believed to heal. In English it goes by the Hankie Tree or the Wishing Tree. It is a terebinth, Pistacia terebinthus, a wild relative of the pistachio, and it grows straight out of the stone of the catacomb complex on Fabrika Hill in Kato Paphos, overhanging a wall above the entrance, with masonry built up around its trunk. Two accounts name the species. On Cyprus the big old terebinths are sometimes the Atlas pistachio instead, so if you can tell the two apart, tell us which this is. Nobody has dated it or measured it either, which is a little odd for a tree with this many visitors. In March it stands bare, the rags the only colour on it, and it was still standing, hung with cloth, when a visitor wrote it up in July 2024. The site is free to enter. That same visitor found the public areas littered and graffitied and the spring entrance roped off, but the tree itself is in plain view from outside the fence, at street level.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the hundreds of strips of cloth hanging from its branches. It grows out of the stone directly above the entrance to the Agia Solomoni catacomb.
trees.access: Free to enter the catacomb site; the tree grows over the catacomb entrance and is seen from the railing at street level. Published hours conflict (daily 08:00 to 16:00, but also closed on Sundays), so check before going.
trees.transport: In Kato Paphos, within walking distance of the harbour area.

trees.name: Aphrodite's Oak

location.address: Junction of the Aphrodite and Adonis nature trails, Akamas peninsula, near Neo Chorio, Paphos District

trees.story: The oak specialist who toured the island's great oaks in spring 2026 called this one the most impressive he met in Cyprus, and it is the one with no story attached. No legend, no chapel, no age anyone has written down. Just a trunk about two metres across and a canopy spreading 28 metres, standing alone in the Mediterranean scrub of the Akamas peninsula, exactly where the Aphrodite and Adonis nature trails fork. Two metres across works out at about 6.3 metres round, calculated from the diameter in the International Oak Society's report rather than taped. It is an Aleppo oak, Quercus infectoria subsp. veneris, and the report describes intact branches and excellent vitality. A walker who passed in October 2026 found it as described, an ancient oak with a very large trunk at the junction, and a hiking app lists it together with a water fountain. The walk to it is part of the point. The trails run through the protected Akamas area, inland from the Baths of Aphrodite west of Polis, and the tree sits near the village of Neo Chorio. Keep to the paths and follow whatever rules are posted at the trailhead. One comment online calls it a French tree, 800 years old, and neither half survives a second look. Nobody has dated it properly. If you know when it was first recorded, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the lone big oak, its trunk about two metres across under a 28-metre canopy. It stands where the Aphrodite and Adonis nature trails fork, near a water fountain.
trees.access: Free and open to walkers on the Aphrodite and Adonis nature trails in the Akamas protected area; no fee or gate found. Reached on foot only; check posted rules for the protected area.
trees.transport: No public transport found. By car to the trailheads near the Baths of Aphrodite and Neo Chorio, roughly 8 km west of Polis, then on foot along the trail to the fork.

trees.name: The Simou village square terebinth
trees.story: The taverna tables in Simou's village square sit in the shade of a tree that may be a thousand years old. A Cyprus Mail reviewer who ate there in 2023 called it colossal and said its shade was complete, and the taverna on the square is O Tremythas, tremithos being the Cypriot word for this kind of tree. It is an Atlas pistachio, Pistacia atlantica, under government protection, and it shares the square with the church of Panagia Chryseleousa, which dominates the village skyline and was built in 1949, making it the newcomer of the two by several centuries at least. Simou, a village of about 170 people in the Paphos hills, has two of these trees on the Department of Forests register. One is 6.15 metres round and 16 metres tall, with an estimated age of about 1,000 years. The other is 4.54 metres round, also 16 metres tall, and about 500. The tree in the square is most likely the bigger one, since local accounts put it at over 1,000 years, but no source says so in writing, so the measurements here are probable rather than proven, and the age somewhere between the two. Every one of those ages is an estimate rather than a ring count. If you know which register tree this is, or where the second one stands, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the big tree whose shade covers the taverna tables in the square. It stands in Simou's village square beside the church of Panagia Chryseleousa.

official_register.name: Μνημεία της φύσης, Τμήμα Δασών (Department of Forests, Cyprus)

trees.access: Free; the tree stands in the public village square beside the church, with a taverna's outdoor tables in its shade.
trees.transport: By car; the village is about 5 km north-west of Fyti in the Paphos hills. Bus service not checked.
